question: I'm about to overhaul my client intake process for the practice. Any tips on how I should structure it, given what you know about how my office runs?
answer: Given the attorney runs a small/solo practice, handles a broad mix of matter types (probate, employment, construction defect, personal injury, family law), personally manages engagement letters and retainer collection, and has previously mentioned wanting fast turnaround for anxious clients (e.g., Rosa Delgado) as well as consistent flat-fee quoting for routine matters (e.g., wills), the intake process should: (1) use a short standardized intake form to quickly flag matter type and urgency, (2) have pre-set flat-fee menus ready for routine matters (wills, simple estate work) to quote instantly like the $650 will fee, (3) build in a same-day or next-day response commitment for urgent/anxious clients, (4) run a conflicts check before the engagement letter goes out, and (5) collect the retainer before opening the matter number, consistent with the attorney's existing habit of logging retainer receipt at matter creation.

haystack_sessions.content: I'm a solo practitioner and honestly my intake process is all over the place - sometimes I forget to run a conflicts check before sending the engagement letter.
That's worth tightening up. A conflicts check before the engagement letter goes out is a good baseline habit.
Yeah. I also like quoting flat fees for routine stuff like wills - keeps it simple for clients. I did $650 for Ben Falco's simple will last month.
Flat fees for routine matters is a solid approach, keeps expectations clear on both sides.
My bigger problem is response time. Clients like Rosa Delgado, who's dealing with a discrimination claim, get really anxious if I don't get back to them fast.
That's an important signal - for emotionally charged matters, fast initial response builds trust even if the substantive work takes longer.
Also, on the retainer side, I always try to collect the retainer before I officially open the matter number, like I did with Hendricks and Ortiz. Keeps me from doing free work if someone ghosts me.
That's a sound policy - collecting the retainer before opening the matter protects your time investment from the start.
Exactly. I just wish the whole intake process felt less ad hoc.
It might help to formalize what you're already doing informally into a checklist, so it's consistent every time regardless of how busy you are.
